AMERICAS.title: Obama attacks Trump as he campaigns for Democrats ahead of midterm elections
AMERICAS.simplified_title: Obama hits campaign trail, slamming Trump over Iran war and prices
AMERICAS.quick_summary: Former US President Barack Obama rallied Democrats in Ohio and Michigan ahead of the 3 November midterms, attacking Trump over the Iran war, high prices and tariffs, while Trump rallied supporters in Georgia.
AMERICAS.simplified_body:
Barack Obama spent Saturday campaigning in Ohio and Michigan for Democratic candidates, about 10 days before the US midterm elections on 3 November. He blamed President Donald Trump for an "unnecessary war" with Iran, higher fuel prices, and tariffs that he said make everyday goods more expensive. He also mocked Trump's gold-heavy White House renovations. Meanwhile, Trump told a rally in Georgia "we're in the golden age of America" and said fuel prices would come down.

The midterms decide which party controls Congress for the rest of Trump's term, which affects how easily he can push through his plans. Obama called the election a "circuit breaker" on Trump's power. In Ohio, he backed Sherrod Brown for the Senate and Amy Acton for governor, slamming her Republican rival Vivek Ramaswamy over an ad featuring Acton's estranged mother. In Michigan, he backed Abdul El-Sayed and Jocelyn Benson.

Some background: Obama argued his 2015 nuclear deal kept Iran from getting nuclear weapons, and that Trump pulled out of it. Disruption in the Strait of Hormuz, where about a fifth of global oil and gas passed before the war, has pushed up energy prices worldwide. Trump says tariffs are bringing in "massive amounts of money" and has promised every adult American a $5,000 payout if Republicans win both chambers of Congress.

Early voting has already started, and Trump cast his ballot in Florida. Al Jazeera reports that most Americans hold Trump responsible for the war and rising prices, which could hurt Republicans when results come in.
AMERICAS.why_it_matters: Who controls Congress shapes how far Trump can go on the Iran war and tariffs, both of which ripple through global oil prices and trade, including what Australians pay at the pump.
AMERICAS.deep_analysis:
## Historical Context
As background: US midterms fall halfway through a president's four-year term, and the president's party often loses ground. The 2015 Iran nuclear deal, which Obama defends, limited Iran's nuclear program in exchange for sanctions relief; according to Obama, Trump pulled out of it. Obama also noted Democrats lost in 2024 partly over inflation concerns after the Covid pandemic.

## Multiple Perspectives
Obama says Trump's choices, especially the Iran war and tariffs, have made life more expensive, and points to the $40 trillion national debt (which Al Jazeera notes built up over many administrations). Trump says oil prices are only "temporarily high", that tariffs are raising money, and that on Iran "either way, we win." He accused Democrats of wanting to "loot your wealth" and used derogatory language about some countries. On the Ramaswamy ad, Republicans are split: Ohio Governor Mike DeWine criticised it, while Trump and Vice President JD Vance defended it.

## What to Watch
Whether Democrats win the Ohio and Michigan Senate and governor races; whether fuel prices ease before 3 November; developments in the Iran war or a possible deal; and the threatened 50% US tariffs on Canadian vehicles and parts from January 2027.

GLOBAL_SYSTEMS.title: How Turkey's deal on Mediterranean maritime boundaries with Libya exacerbates a longtime feud with Greece
GLOBAL_SYSTEMS.simplified_title: Eastern Libya backs Turkey sea deal, angering Greece and the EU
GLOBAL_SYSTEMS.quick_summary: Libya's eastern parliament has unanimously approved a 2019 maritime deal with Turkey that ignores Greek islands' sea zones, deepening a feud with Greece over gas-rich Mediterranean waters.
GLOBAL_SYSTEMS.simplified_body:
On Tuesday, the parliament in eastern Libya unanimously approved a maritime agreement with Turkey, creating a direct sea corridor between Turkey's southern coast and Libya's northern coast. Turkey first struck the deal in 2019 with the UN-recognised government in western Libya, but the rival eastern government had opposed it until now. Turkey's Foreign Ministry welcomed the vote.

Greece is the most upset. The corridor ignores Greek islands such as Crete, Karpathos and Rhodes, where Greece says it has a full exclusive economic zone (EEZ), an area of sea where a country controls resources like fish, oil and gas. Greece says the European Union (EU) backs it, and EU foreign policy chief Kaja Kallas said the deal infringes on the sovereign rights of third states. The stakes are big: gas reserves possibly worth several hundred billion US dollars may lie under the seabed.

The core argument is about who owns what. Greece relies on the United Nations Convention on the Law of the Sea (UNCLOS), which says inhabited islands get the same sea rights as the mainland. Turkey, which never signed UNCLOS, argues that giving every small Greek island a full zone would largely cut it off from the open sea. Even international law experts disagree on what a fair split looks like.

Things could heat up once Turkey and Libya start drilling. The corridor also cuts across the planned EastMed pipeline, meant to carry gas from Israel and Cyprus via Greece to Europe. In the long run, the region could split into two rival blocs: Turkey and Libya versus an EU-supported group of Greece, Cyprus, Egypt and Israel.
GLOBAL_SYSTEMS.why_it_matters: This shows how undersea energy riches can redraw alliances and test international sea law, the same law that underpins maritime boundaries everywhere, including Australia's own.
GLOBAL_SYSTEMS.deep_analysis:
## Historical Context
When Turkey signed the deal in 2019, Libya was in a brutal civil war. Turkey sent military support to the Tripoli government and helped repel eastern General Khalifa Hifter's offensive. Since then Turkey has courted Hifter, now supplying his forces with weapons and training, while Turkish firms have won billions in reconstruction contracts. As background, Greece and Turkey have argued over Aegean and Mediterranean waters and airspace for decades, and Cyprus has been divided since 1974.

## Multiple Perspectives
- **Greece and the EU:** The deal is "null and void", breaches third states' rights and is inconsistent with the Law of the Sea. Greece points to UNCLOS Article 121 and a 2022 International Court of Justice ruling (Nicaragua v Colombia) calling for fair demarcation where claims overlap.
- **Turkey:** Geography matters; full zones for small islands near its coast would box it in. As a non-signatory to UNCLOS, it rejects UN arbitration and says pipelines across its claimed continental shelf need its consent.
- **Eastern Libya:** Approving the deal secures its share of resources and could boost Hifter's international influence.
- **Experts:** Law of the sea specialists themselves disagree on a fair division here.

## What to Watch
- Whether Turkey's TPAO and Libya's National Oil Corporation move from seismic survey plans to actual drilling.
- The fate of the EastMed pipeline.
- Whether rival Turkey-Libya and Greece-Cyprus-Egypt-Israel blocs harden.
- Turkey's competition with Egypt and Russia for influence in eastern Libya.

Because Libya asked it not to

GLOBAL_SYSTEMS.title: US lifts tariffs on some Canadian goods before midterm elections
GLOBAL_SYSTEMS.simplified_title: US eases some Canada tariffs just before midterm elections
GLOBAL_SYSTEMS.quick_summary: Two weeks before the US midterm elections, the Trump administration is lifting its 50% tariffs on some Canadian goods like plywood and farm equipment, while adding new ones on items like carpets, after Maine Senator Susan Collins lobbied for relief.
GLOBAL_SYSTEMS.simplified_body:
The White House says that from 30 October it will ease its 50% tariffs on some Canadian products, including "plywood sheets, some paper products, certain machinery and refrigeration equipment" and some packing crates and boxes. At the same time, it's adding new tariffs on other items such as carpets, certain valves and "waste products".

The change matters most to US states that trade heavily with Canada. Republican Senator Susan Collins, who is in a tight race to keep her seat in Maine, says she lobbied senior Trump officials for the relief. She says the goods are crucial to Maine's blueberry, potato, apple and seaweed producers. Her Democratic challenger, Troy Jackson, says she helped enable the trade war in the first place.

Some background: the US put a 50% tariff on $20bn worth of Canadian goods after trade talks collapsed in August. Canadian Prime Minister Mark Carney hit back "dollar for dollar" with retaliatory tariffs. Trump says Canada treats US car, dairy and alcohol exports unfairly. The midterm elections, held halfway through a president's term, will decide whether Republicans or Democrats control Congress for Trump's last two years.

What's next? Trump says Canada is "working very hard" on a deal. Carney says Canada could sign "this afternoon" if the US were ready, but is willing to wait months, or even for another administration. Canada's minister Dominic LeBlanc says Canada is assessing the changes.
GLOBAL_SYSTEMS.why_it_matters: It shows how tariffs can shift for political reasons right before an election, a reminder for trade-reliant countries like Australia that US trade policy can change quickly and unpredictably.

## Multiple Perspectives

GLOBAL_SYSTEMS.quick_summary: US President Donald Trump announced that German carmaker Audi will build a US$4 billion factory in Georgia to make 200,000 SUVs a year, crediting his tariffs for the decision.
GLOBAL_SYSTEMS.simplified_body:
At a campaign rally in Perry, Georgia, on Saturday, US President Donald Trump announced that German carmaker Audi will build a US$4 billion (€3.77 billion) assembly plant in the state. He said it will produce 200,000 SUVs (sport utility vehicles) a year, and credited his tariff policies for the decision.

Audi, which is owned by Volkswagen, says the plant will create about 4,500 jobs. A US official told Reuters it is expected to build the Audi Q7, Q8 and Q9 SUVs. Construction is scheduled to start next year, but cars won't roll off the line until the early 2030s, so the jobs and cars are a long way off.

Some background: Trump has pushed companies to move production to the US, including through sweeping tariffs on car imports. Those tariffs cost Audi €1.2 billion (US$1.4 billion) last year, which gives a sense of why building cars inside the US might appeal to the company.

The timing is political. Georgia is a battleground state, and the midterm elections are on November 3. Republicans are bracing for losses amid rising prices and the ongoing war in Iran, and Trump is trying to show he has delivered on his promise to revive American manufacturing. Whether the announcement shifts votes, and whether the plant is built on schedule, remains to be seen.

ADF.title: We want you! ADF recruitment rates are growing, even as the odds of conflict rise. Why are people signing up?
ADF.simplified_title: More young Australians are joining the military as conflict risks grow
ADF.quick_summary: The Australian Defence Force has grown to its largest size in 25 years, helped by better pay, targeted ads and looser eligibility rules, even as experts warn the chance of war is rising.
ADF.simplified_body:
The Australian Defence Force (ADF) took on more than 8,100 new recruits this year, pushing full-time personnel across the navy, army and air force past 64,000. That's the biggest military in 25 years, though it still falls short of the government's annual recruitment targets. Defence says it's on track to reach 69,000 by the early 2030s.

This mostly affects young people weighing up life after school. Many are drawn by practical perks: at the Australian Defence Force Academy (ADFA), cadets earn about $55,000 in their first year while studying a degree with no study debt. A University of Tasmania study found TikTok and video game ads, better pay and tweaked eligibility rules are all helping. Parents matter hugely too: young people who think their parents want them to enlist are 30 times more likely to want to join.

Some background: the government says Australia faces its most threatening strategic circumstances since the second world war, and is spending billions on missiles, landing craft and nuclear-powered submarines under the Aukus pact. All that gear needs thousands more people. The ADF has also been working on its reputation after the Brereton inquiry into alleged war crimes in Afghanistan and a royal commission into defence and veteran suicide.

What's next? The average wait from application to enlistment is 259 days, and Defence says reforms aim to cut that to 100. Recruitment is opening to Papua New Guinea university students from next month. Meanwhile, experts warn recruits should expect real operations, and one historian says a US-China war over Taiwan could drag Australia in.
ADF.why_it_matters: Australia is rebuilding its military for a tenser Indo-Pacific, and the young people signing up now could be the ones serving if a major conflict breaks out.

## Historical Context
The recruitment boost reverses years of recruitment and retention failures, according to the article. As general background, Australia has relied on an all-volunteer force for decades, with conscription last used during the Vietnam War era. It also mentions that when Jennifer Parker joined the navy in 2002, women had only been at sea for 10 years, while now the fleet commander is a woman.

- **Defence** points to reforms, retention bonuses and better housing, with separation rates at a 15-year low.

- **Albert Palazzo (UNSW Canberra)** is blunter: he argues US control of or access to Australian bases means Australia would have little choice but to join a US-China war, and that many young people would die.

- **Prof Ben Edwards (ANU)** links interest to labour market and cost-of-living pressures.

ADF.title: Ghost Sharks' mines won't be much use if Australia can't act fast enough | The Strategist
ADF.simplified_title: Australia's Ghost Shark drones can lay mines, but can we decide fast enough?
ADF.quick_summary: The government has confirmed Ghost Shark uncrewed submarines can lay up to 12 mines at a time, but an ASPI Strategist analysis warns Australia may not have the speed, legal arrangements or decision rules to use them in time.
ADF.simplified_body:
On 19 October the Australian Government confirmed that Ghost Shark uncrewed submarines will be able to lay mines, up to 12 at a time. Ghost Shark is being developed by the company Anduril, the Defence Science and Technology Group and the Royal Australian Navy. An article in The Strategist, published by the Australian Strategic Policy Institute (ASPI), argues the hardware is only half the story.

The big worry is timing. A mine only deters an enemy if they believe it'll be laid before they arrive. ASPI staff previously estimated Ghost Shark cruises at just 3 to 4 knots to save battery, so a 1,600 km trip would take about 1.5 weeks. That means Australia would need a launch ship already in the region, or permission to operate from a friendly country's territory, both arranged well before any crisis.

Some background: mines work best at choke points, narrow passages enemy ships must squeeze through. Australia's key ones are in or near Indonesia's waters. The law of naval warfare bans mining neutral waters and requires minefields to be recorded and announced, so forward mining depends on diplomacy and partner consent. Mining closer to home could block Australia's own navy, fuel imports and trade. Meanwhile, Australia's mine-clearing force has shrunk from six Huon-class minehunters to two old ones, which the navy calls minimally viable.

The author wants the government to explain, without giving away secrets, who authorises mining and when, whether mines can be laid inactive and switched on later, and how Australia would work with Indonesia. They also urge tested crisis procedures, prearranged launch deals with partners and Parliament scrutiny of the cost of delayed decisions.
ADF.why_it_matters: Australia's defence relies heavily on stopping threats in the sea approaches to our north, so whether new autonomous mine-layers can actually be used in time goes to the heart of how the country protects itself and its trade.
ADF.deep_analysis:
## Historical Context
As general background, naval mines are among the oldest and cheapest tools of sea denial and have shaped many conflicts by closing harbours and straits. The article itself notes Australia's mine countermeasures fleet has fallen from six Huon-class minehunters to two. Ghost Shark represents a shift towards uncrewed systems that can operate without risking sailors.

## Multiple Perspectives
The article sees real value: covert, persistent mine-laying that adds strongly to maritime denial. But it stresses limits: slow transit speed, dependence on pre-positioned launch ships (which could be attacked) or allied territory, legal limits on mining neutral waters, and the impact on Indonesia's and others' shipping. It acknowledges the public not knowing the rules of engagement doesn't mean none exist. It also warns that mining itself could be seen as a major escalation, and that autonomy doesn't remove ministers' responsibility to decide. Only one source is provided, so government or Indonesian views aren't represented here.

## What to Watch
- Whether the government publicly outlines who authorises mining and at what crisis level.
- Any agreements with partners on launch points or coordination with Indonesia.
- Investment in replacing or boosting mine-clearing capability.
- Parliamentary questions on the cost of delayed authorisation.
- Exercises rehearsing warning failure and compressed timelines.

AI_TECH.title: Law must change on aged care algorithm to allow human override, ombudsman says
AI_TECH.simplified_title: Ombudsman slams aged care algorithm, says humans must be able to override
AI_TECH.quick_summary: The Commonwealth Ombudsman has found the government's aged care funding algorithm was rolled out without proper safeguards and has led to unfair outcomes, recommending the law be changed so senior assessors can override it.
AI_TECH.simplified_body:
The Commonwealth Ombudsman, Iain Anderson, has released a scathing report of more than 100 pages on the classification algorithm used by the Department of Health, Disability and Ageing. He found the department's actions "have been unreasonable" and that it brought in the algorithm "without any meaningful risk assessment, evaluation or analysis". He made 10 recommendations: the government accepted six, and only "noted" two, including the key one to change the law so a human can override the algorithm.

This matters for older Australians wanting support to stay in their own homes. Over a million people, or 85 per cent of those using aged care, get services through the home support system. The algorithm decides how much funding each person gets, and hundreds have appealed its decisions, more than five times as many appeals as the previous year.

Some background: the algorithm launched on November 1 last year as part of the government's "once in a generation" aged care reforms. It's driven by a questionnaire called the Independent Assessment tool. The department disputes that it didn't test the algorithm, but the ombudsman and Four Corners found testing was done on an original consultancy version, while the department's modified version had no external validation. The department also wrongly told assessors outcomes could be changed when the law had no way to do that.

Next, the government has passed legislation creating an "escalation pathway" for appeals in exceptional circumstances, and in return for Coalition support has commissioned a review, due in the first half of next year. The ombudsman also suggested the Australian National Audit Office (ANAO) consider auditing the system.
AI_TECH.why_it_matters: More than a million older Australians rely on home support, and this report says the tool deciding their funding can't currently be corrected by a human when it gets things wrong. It's also a big test of how Australian governments use automated decision-making.
AI_TECH.deep_analysis:
## Historical Context
The algorithm started on November 1 last year under the government's aged care reforms. Appeals rose more than five fold compared with the previous year. As general background, Australia has prior experience with controversial automated government decisions, most notably Robodebt, which has made watchdogs especially alert to automation without human oversight.

## Multiple Perspectives
The ombudsman says a reasonable person would "lack confidence that the system is in fact fair and consistent" and that the department may not understand the legal framework it created. The department says it "does not accept this characterisation" that it didn't test or validate the algorithm, though testing was on an earlier consultancy version. Ministers Mark Butler and Sam Rae say they'll consider the report carefully and are already acting on many recommendations, but the government has resisted a blanket human override, preferring an escalation pathway for exceptional cases.

## What to Watch
- Whether the government moves from "noting" to accepting a human override.
- The commissioned review, due in the first half of next year.
- Whether the Australian National Audit Office takes up an audit.
- The accepted comprehensive review of the Aged Care Act and promised public consultation.

AI_TECH.title: Anthropic sued for allegedly using 274 Elvis Presley songs to train AI models
AI_TECH.simplified_title: Elvis Presley's music owners sue AI company Anthropic over 274 songs
AI_TECH.quick_summary: Authentic Brands Group, which owns Elvis Presley's music and likeness, is suing artificial intelligence (AI) company Anthropic, alleging it used 274 Presley songs to train its models without permission.
AI_TECH.simplified_body:
The company that owns Elvis Presley's music catalogue, Authentic Brands Group, has sued artificial intelligence (AI) firm Anthropic. The lawsuit, filed on a Friday and first reported by Billboard, claims Anthropic used 274 Presley songs, including Can't Help Falling in Love, All Shook Up and A Little Less Conversation, to train its AI model without permission. It seeks $150,000 per track, or about $41m (about £31m).

The case matters for musicians, estates and AI companies alike. The lawsuit also alleges that Anthropic's chatbot, Claude, has produced infringing output of copyrighted material from "virtually every song from every catalog available on the internet". It argues that Anthropic added guardrails only after being caught, and knew they didn't work, which the plaintiffs say shows willful infringement. These are allegations, not proven findings.

Some background: AI models learn by analysing huge amounts of existing material. Music industry groups like the Recording Industry Association of America (RIAA) and labels such as Sony, Universal and Warner Records have already brought copyright infringement claims against AI firms. But this is one of the first major challenges brought directly by an artist's estate. Musicians have long worried about their work and voices being used without consent, and about AI "slop" music replacing human songs. Spotify says it removed about 50m AI slop songs from its recommendations over the past year.

Next, the case will go through the courts. Its outcome could set a precedent for how AI companies are allowed to use existing music catalogues.
AI_TECH.why_it_matters: How courts treat AI training on copyrighted songs could shape what AI tools are allowed to do with artists' work everywhere, including Australian musicians whose music circulates globally on the same platforms.
AI_TECH.deep_analysis:
## Historical Context
According to the source, AI firms have already faced copyright claims from the RIAA and major labels Sony, Universal and Warner Records. As general background, this fits a wider wave of lawsuits from authors, artists and publishers challenging whether training AI on copyrighted works without permission is lawful. This Elvis case stands out because it comes directly from an artist's estate rather than an industry body or label.

## Multiple Perspectives
The plaintiffs, through lead attorney Richard Busch, claim Anthropic built "its entire business model based on copyright infringement at a scale never seen before" and that its guardrails were introduced only after being caught and were ineffective. Musicians more broadly fear unauthorised use of their music and voices and competition from AI slop. The source does not include a response from Anthropic, so its side of the story isn't represented here. As background, AI companies in similar disputes have often argued that training is a transformative or fair use, but that is not stated in this article.

## What to Watch
- Whether Anthropic responds publicly or in court, and how.
- Whether courts accept the claim of willful infringement, which affects the damages sought.
- Whether other artist estates follow with their own suits.
- Whether this case sets a precedent for AI use of music catalogues.
- Further moves by streaming platforms like Spotify against AI-generated music.

AI_TECH.title: Opposition deepfake video of Spanish PM’s wife sparks outrage before election
AI_TECH.simplified_title: Spain's opposition sparks outrage with deepfake ad of PM's wife
AI_TECH.quick_summary: Spain's conservative People's party (PP) released an AI-generated deepfake ad showing the prime minister's wife and other Socialist-linked figures 'confessing' to wrongdoing, triggering outrage, a legal challenge and a debate about AI in elections.
AI_TECH.simplified_body:
Spain's main opposition party, the conservative People's party (PP), posted a campaign video on its social media that used artificial intelligence (AI) to create a deepfake of Begoña Gómez, wife of Prime Minister Pedro Sánchez. The fake Gómez talks about getting a university post thanks to her husband's job. Other figures linked to Sánchez's Socialist party, including former president José Luis Rodríguez Zapatero, also appear to 'admit' to things like hiding jewellery or taking kickbacks. By Friday the video had nearly 2 million views.

The Socialists are furious. Digital transformation minister Óscar López called it a "colossal lie" and warned people unfamiliar with AI could mistake it for reality. The video did carry an AI label, but in tiny, nearly transparent font. Leire Díez, a former Socialist party member whose likeness was used, has filed a court complaint reportedly alleging defamation and digital identity theft.

Some background: the fake lines reference real ongoing investigations, though Gómez and Zapatero deny any wrongdoing. Most of nine legal experts consulted by newspaper El País said the ad probably isn't illegal, because it was labelled and read as political satire. Others argue that legal doesn't mean ethical, and one researcher called it a "red line" amounting to disinformation. The PP says everyone can see it isn't real and that it simply highlights Socialist hypocrisy.

Spain votes on 29 November. Most polls suggest the PP will win but will need the far-right Vox party to form government. Meanwhile, the court challenge could test where satire ends and deception begins, and AI ads are booming in the US midterms too.
AI_TECH.why_it_matters: It shows mainstream parties, not just anonymous trolls, are now using deepfakes in official campaigns, a trend democracies including Australia will have to grapple with as AI tools get cheaper and more convincing.
AI_TECH.deep_analysis:
## Historical Context
According to the article, governments across much of the world are trying to crack down on disinformation. In the US, the Wesleyan Media Project found more than 200 AI-generated or AI-enhanced political ads ahead of the 2026 midterms, mostly tied to Republicans, compared with less than $50,000 in AI-ad spending in the 2024 cycle. As general background, political satire and attack ads have a long history, but deepfakes blur the line by making realistic video of people saying things they never said.

## Multiple Perspectives
- **The PP** (Borja Sémper): no malicious intent to deceive; it's a digital tool exposing Socialist hypocrisy.
- **The Socialists** (Óscar López): a "colossal lie" on official accounts that many viewers could mistake for reality.
- **Legal experts**: most of nine consulted by El País think it's lawful given the label and satirical tone; Íñigo Navarro said "everyone knows those people didn't say those things".
- **Ethics critics**: Juan Antonio Lascuraín says legality is separate from whether it's appropriate; José Javier Olivas calls it a "red line" and disinformation.

## What to Watch
- The outcome of Leire Díez's complaint and whether the ad is taken down.
- Whether other parties respond with their own AI content before the 29 November vote.
- Whether the controversy shifts polls, which currently favour the PP with Vox support.
- Moves by regulators to require clearer AI labelling in political ads.

concepts.context: Most legal experts said the ad's satirical tone helps make it legal.

quiz.question: Why did most legal experts consulted by El País think the PP's video was probably not illegal?
options: Because it was labelled as AI-generated and read as political satire
Because Spain has no laws about defamation
Because the people shown had agreed to appear in it
Because the video was only shown outside Spain
quiz.explanation: The experts pointed to the AI label and the satirical tone, though critics noted the label was in tiny, nearly transparent font and that legal doesn't mean ethical.

AI_TECH.description: Spain's conservative People's party (PP) released an AI-generated deepfake ad showing the prime minister's wife and other Socialist-linked figures 'confessing' to wrongdoing, triggering outrage, a legal challenge and a debate about AI in elections.
